# ISLA, one idea at a time {#sec-isla}

*Before this chapter:* @sec-problem (the boundary-to-field operator and the
running airfoil) and @sec-landscape (attention as a kernel integral
operator, slice attention, the transformer block). Nothing about ISLA is
assumed.

**ISLA is a slice-attention transformer that never sees a coordinate.**
Every learned operation inside it acts on scalars that do not change when
the body is rotated, translated or uniformly rescaled. Every sum it takes
over the boundary is a quadrature rule, so its answer converges to one field
as the mesh is refined, wherever the mesher put its cells. Vectors and
tensors are rebuilt at the very end, from directions that rotate with the
body. That is the whole design. This chapter builds it up in seven ideas,
each with a picture on the two-dimensional airfoil of @sec-problem.
@fig-isla-overview is the map.

The chapter carries no accuracy numbers. What the design buys and costs in
measured error is the business of Part IV; the two properties it is built
for are tested in @sec-invariances; the exact computation, with every tensor
shape and code identifier, is @sec-architecture. Collapsed notes hold
derivations and code correspondences, and the text reads completely with all
of them closed.

```{python}
#| label: setup-isla
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
from matplotlib.collections import LineCollection
from matplotlib.colors import Normalize

# The running example at three resolutions, and an uneven "mesher": fine at the leading edge, coarse elsewhere.
Ju = joukowski(n_cells=40)
u_ = np.linspace(0, 1, 2001)
density = 1.0 + 14.0 * np.exp(-((u_ - 0.5) / 0.05) ** 2) + 2.0 * np.exp(-(u_ / 0.04) ** 2) + 2.0 * np.exp(-((u_ - 1.0) / 0.04) ** 2)
cdf = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(density[:-1] * np.diff(u_))]); cdf /= cdf[-1]
Jm = joukowski(n_cells=40, frac=np.interp(np.linspace(0, 1, 41), cdf, u_))
JJ = joukowski(n_cells=80)

# Six hand-made soft slices on the 80-cell airfoil: logits that prefer a stretch of arclength.
s_arc = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(JJ["w"])]); s_mid = (s_arc[:-1] + s_arc[1:]) / 2; total = s_arc[-1]
N_SL = 6
centers = (np.arange(N_SL) + 0.5) / N_SL * total
dd = np.abs(s_mid[:, None] - centers[None, :]); dd = np.minimum(dd, total - dd)
width6 = np.array([0.06, 0.06, 0.06, 0.13, 0.06, 0.06])[None, :]     # the slice at the leading edge wraps it
logits6 = -(dd / (width6 * total)) ** 2
a6 = np.exp(logits6 + np.log(JJ["w"])[:, None]); a6 /= a6.sum(axis=0, keepdims=True)   # softmax over points, measure bias
z6 = (a6[:, :, None] * JJ["mid"][:, None, :]).sum(axis=0)                                # anchor positions
m6 = (a6[:, :, None] * JJ["nrm"][:, None, :]).sum(axis=0); m6 /= np.linalg.norm(m6, axis=1, keepdims=True)
SIX = plt.get_cmap("Dark2")(np.linspace(0, 1, 8))[[0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6]]

def arrow(ax, p, v, c, lw=1.8, z=5):
    return ax.annotate("", xy=p + v, xytext=p, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=c, lw=lw), zorder=z)

def airfoil(ax, J, color=BASELINE, lw=1.2):
    ax.plot(J["xy"][:, 0], J["xy"][:, 1], color=color, lw=lw, zorder=1)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-overview
#| fig-cap: >
#|   ISLA in four pictures, on the running airfoil. (a) What goes in: each
#|   boundary cell becomes a token with a position, a unit normal (gray
#|   arrow) and a measure weight (the cell's length, drawn as the stroke
#|   width); the far-field direction $\hat g_1$ is the one global input.
#|   (b) A slice layer groups the tokens softly into slices (colors) and
#|   gives each slice an anchor (star) with its own mean normal (arrow).
#|   (c) A token learns where it is only from a few scalars against each
#|   anchor: distances and cosines, never coordinates. (d) What comes out:
#|   a vector field (here a made-up surface traction) assembled from
#|   directions the token owns, with learned scalar coefficients, so the
#|   prediction on the rotated airfoil (right) is the rotated prediction. How
#|   to read this: every panel is a schematic with hand-made weights; no
#|   trained model is drawn. Ideas 1 to 7 below take the panels one at a time.
#| code-fold: true
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(9.0, 5.2), gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.08, wspace=0.05))
for ax in axes.flat:
    clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.45, 2.45); ax.set_ylim(-1.35, 1.35)
# (a) tokens
ax = axes[0, 0]
segs = np.stack([Jm["xy"][:-1], Jm["xy"][1:]], axis=1)
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs, colors=[BASELINE], linewidths=1.0 + 5 * Jm["w"] / Jm["w"].max(), capstyle="butt", zorder=1))
ax.quiver(Jm["mid"][:, 0], Jm["mid"][:, 1], Jm["nrm"][:, 0], Jm["nrm"][:, 1], color=MUTED, scale=16, width=0.004, zorder=3)
ax.plot(Jm["mid"][:, 0], Jm["mid"][:, 1], "o", ms=2.6, color=INK, zorder=4)
arrow(ax, np.array([-2.25, 0.95]), 0.7 * Jm["g_hat"], INK, 2.0)
ax.text(-2.3, 1.2, r"$\hat g_1$", fontsize=11, color=INK)
ax.set_title("(a) tokens: position, normal, measure", fontsize=9.5)
# (b) slices and anchors
ax = axes[0, 1]
segs = np.stack([JJ["xy"][:-1], JJ["xy"][1:]], axis=1)
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs, colors=[SIX[k] for k in a6.argmax(axis=1)], linewidths=6, capstyle="butt", zorder=2))
for k in range(N_SL):
    ax.plot(*z6[k], marker="*", ms=14, color=SIX[k], mec=INK, mew=0.6, zorder=5)
    arrow(ax, z6[k], 0.38 * m6[k], SIX[k], 1.6)
ax.set_title("(b) soft slices and their anchors", fontsize=9.5)
# (c) invariants of one token against the anchors
ax = axes[1, 0]
airfoil(ax, JJ)
i0 = 22; xi = JJ["mid"][i0]
for k in range(N_SL):
    ax.plot([xi[0], z6[k, 0]], [xi[1], z6[k, 1]], color=SIX[k], lw=1.0, alpha=0.8, zorder=2)
    ax.plot(*z6[k], marker="*", ms=11, color=SIX[k], mec=INK, mew=0.5, zorder=5)
ax.plot(*xi, "o", ms=7, color=INK, zorder=6); arrow(ax, xi, 0.45 * JJ["nrm"][i0], INK)
ax.text(0.0, -1.22, r"only $|r_i - z_s|$ and cosines, per anchor", ha="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2)
ax.set_title("(c) position as relations to the anchors", fontsize=9.5)
# (d) an output vector field assembled from body-fixed directions, and the same on the rotated airfoil
ax = axes[1, 1]
tang = np.stack([-JJ["nrm"][:, 1], JJ["nrm"][:, 0]], axis=1)
coef_t = 0.35 * np.sin(np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, len(JJ["w"]), endpoint=False)) + 0.15   # invariant coefficients
coef_n = 0.25 * (JJ["cp_s"] - JJ["cp_s"].mean())
vec = coef_t[:, None] * tang + coef_n[:, None] * JJ["nrm"]
th = np.deg2rad(35); Rm = np.array([[np.cos(th), -np.sin(th)], [np.sin(th), np.cos(th)]])
for P, V, col, lw in ((JJ["mid"] * 0.5 + [-1.2, 0.1], vec * 0.5, BLUE, 1.0), (JJ["mid"] @ Rm.T * 0.5 + [1.2, 0.1], vec @ Rm.T * 0.5, BLUE, 0.9)):
    ax.plot(*np.r_[P, P[:1]].T, color=BASELINE, lw=1.0, zorder=1)
    ax.quiver(P[::3, 0], P[::3, 1], V[::3, 0], V[::3, 1], color=col, scale=2.2, width=0.006, zorder=3)
ax.annotate("", xy=(0.55, 0.75), xytext=(-0.55, 0.75), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=MUTED, lw=1.2, connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.3"))
ax.text(0.0, 1.05, "rotate by 35°", ha="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2)
ax.text(0.0, -1.22, "same coefficients, rotated basis", ha="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2)
ax.set_title("(d) outputs from an equivariant basis", fontsize=9.5)
plt.show()
```

## From Transolver to ISLA: what changes {#sec-isla-position}

**ISLA keeps the slice attention of the Transolver family and changes
what the network is allowed to see.** @sec-landscape introduced slice
attention: every token is routed softly into a few hundred slices, the
slices exchange information, and the result is read back to the tokens. It
is the cheapest form of global attention that still learns its own
partition of the domain. Transolver and GeoTransolver feed it
raw coordinates in the dataset's frame and the global conditions as raw
feature columns, so both learn the physics of pose from data, and both
average over whatever points the mesher produced. @tbl-isla-vs-transolver
puts the three side by side.

| | Transolver | GeoTransolver | ISLA |
|---|---|---|---|
| what a learned layer reads about position | coordinates $x_i$ in the dataset frame | coordinates, plus multi-scale neighborhood features and a global geometry context | distances and cosines to slice anchors; no coordinate ever |
| a slice average | over points (count-weighted) | over points | over measure (a quadrature) |
| a vector or tensor output | its components in the dataset frame | its components in the dataset frame | invariant coefficients times body-fixed basis vectors |
| a rigid motion of the input | must be learned (or augmented) | must be learned | changes nothing: exact by construction |
| a change of mesh at fixed geometry | changes the averages | changes the averages | changes the averages by quadrature error only |

: The three architectures of this book on the five things that distinguish
them. How to read this: the table compares what each architecture is built
to do, not how accurate it is; the accuracy comparison is Part IV.
{#tbl-isla-vs-transolver}

The change is paid once, at the network's edges: invariant scalars on the
way in, an equivariant basis on the way out. Inside, a slice layer is the
same kind of object as Transolver's, with two additions this chapter
explains: the routing weights carry the surface measure, and every token
knows where it is only relative to the slice anchors. The opposite design,
which enforces symmetry inside every layer with typed scalar and vector
channels (the tensor-field networks of @sec-landscape), pays the price at
every layer instead of once.

## What goes in and what comes out {#sec-isla-inputs}

**ISLA maps a sampled boundary and the problem's global conditions to
fields at prediction points.** Per case, the inputs are:

- $N$ sampled boundary cells, each a **token** with a position
  $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ (its centroid), a unit normal $\hat n_i$ and a
  **measure weight** $w_i > 0$, the area (in two dimensions, the length) the
  cell stands for, so that $\sum_i w_i f(x_i) \approx \int f\,dA$. Under the
  scoring protocol of @sec-protocol, $N = 200{,}000$ per case.
- **Global vector inputs** $g_1, \dots, g_K$: directions that belong to the
  problem rather than to any cell. External aerodynamics has $K = 1$, the
  far-field flow direction; a buoyant flow would add gravity, a magnetized
  one the applied field; steady conduction with prescribed temperatures has
  $K = 0$. Each enters as a unit direction $\hat g_k$. A magnitude that
  matters is a global scalar.
- **Global scalar inputs** $\sigma \in \mathbb{R}^S$: parameters of the PDE
  such as a Reynolds number or an inlet speed.
- Optionally, per-cell **boundary data** (a condition tag, a prescribed
  traction, a Dirichlet value) and per-point **query data** (a material
  label), as named fields of declared tensor rank.
- For an interior task, the **prediction points** $x_q$ and nothing else
  about them. The wall distance and direction a prediction point needs are
  functions of the boundary and the point, so ISLA computes them itself
  (idea 7).

The outputs are named fields of declared rank at the prediction points:
scalars (pressure, von Mises stress), vectors (wall shear stress,
velocity), and tensors up to rank 4 (a stress tensor). On a surface task
the prediction points *are* the boundary cells. @fig-isla-inputs shows
everything one token carries.

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-inputs
#| fig-cap: >
#|   What one token carries, on the running airfoil with an uneven mesh
#|   (fine at the leading edge, coarse elsewhere). Each boundary cell (black
#|   dot at its midpoint) has a position, a unit outward normal (gray arrow)
#|   and a measure weight, drawn as the thickness of the segment. The one
#|   global input is the far-field direction (black arrow). How to read this:
#|   nothing else enters the model; in particular no coordinate of any point
#|   is ever given to a learned layer.
#| code-fold: true
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 3.6))
clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.5, 2.6); ax.set_ylim(-1.3, 1.5)
segs = np.stack([Jm["xy"][:-1], Jm["xy"][1:]], axis=1)
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs, colors=[BASELINE], linewidths=2 + 14 * Jm["w"] / Jm["w"].max(), capstyle="butt", zorder=1))
ax.plot(Jm["xy"][:, 0], Jm["xy"][:, 1], color=INK, lw=0.8, zorder=2)
ax.quiver(Jm["mid"][:, 0], Jm["mid"][:, 1], Jm["nrm"][:, 0], Jm["nrm"][:, 1], color=MUTED, scale=12, width=0.0035, headwidth=4, zorder=3)
ax.plot(Jm["mid"][:, 0], Jm["mid"][:, 1], "o", ms=3.2, color=INK, zorder=4)
ax.annotate(r"token $i$: position $x_i$, normal $\hat n_i$, measure $w_i$", xy=Jm["mid"][8], xytext=(0.2, -1.15),
            fontsize=9.5, color=INK, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=INK2, lw=0.8))
arrow(ax, np.array([-1.9, 1.05]), 0.8 * Jm["g_hat"], INK, 2.0)
ax.text(-2.4, 1.3, r"global direction $\hat g_1$ (far-field flow)", fontsize=9.5, color=INK)
ax.text(1.05, 0.95, "thick segment: large measure weight\n(a coarse cell); thin: a fine cell", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Optional: the call signature"}
Every constructor argument and every `forward` input is keyword-only. Each
field other than the geometry is named and carries a declared rank in the
grammar every mesh model of the library shares
(`physicsnemo.mesh.fields.FieldSchema`): `{"rank": r, "symmetric": bool,
"parity": "even" | "odd"}`. The constructor takes `output_schema`,
`boundary_schema`, `query_schema` and `global_schema`. `forward` takes
`boundary_meshes`, a mapping from a name to a codimension-one `Mesh` whose
cells are the tokens (centroid, normal, measure) with the boundary fields in
its `cell_data`; `global_data`, with a rank-1 field as a `(d,)` vector and a
rank-0 field as a scalar; and, for an interior task, `prediction_points`, a
point cloud with the query fields in its `point_data`. It returns a
point-cloud `Mesh` whose `point_data` holds the outputs, shaped `(N,)`,
`(N, d)`, `(N, d, d)` by rank. A dotted name (`surface.pressure`) is a
nested group. @sec-using-inputs is the operating manual for all of this.
:::

## Idea 1: every sum over the boundary is a quadrature rule {#sec-isla-quadrature}

**A mesh is a discretization of a surface, not the surface itself, so any
quantity the model forms by summing over cells must be an integral estimate
that does not care how the cells were laid down.** A plain mean over points
depends on the mesher: refine the leading edge and the mean of anything is
pulled toward the leading edge. A measure-weighted mean,
$\sum_i w_i f_i / \sum_i w_i$, estimates $\int f\,dA / \int dA$, and every
consistent mesh gives the same number up to quadrature error.
@fig-isla-quadrature shows the difference: two meshers, one shape, two plain
means, one weighted mean.

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-quadrature
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Two samplings of one airfoil, and the mean pressure coefficient each
#|   gives. Left: equal-arclength cells. Right: the same shape with cells
#|   clustered at the leading edge, as a mesher resolving the suction peak
#|   would. Color is the potential-flow surface pressure coefficient. The
#|   plain mean over points (gray) moves between the two samplings because
#|   the second has more points where the pressure is low; the
#|   measure-weighted mean (blue) is a quadrature of the same integral and
#|   moves only by the quadrature error. How to read this: every slice sum
#|   inside ISLA is of the blue kind. It does not show a trained model.
#| code-fold: true
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.4, 3.9))
norm = mpl.colors.TwoSlopeNorm(vcenter=0.0, vmin=-1.6, vmax=1.0)
for ax, J, title in zip(axes, (Ju, Jm), ("equal-arclength sampling", "leading-edge-clustered sampling")):
    clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.4, 2.4); ax.set_ylim(-1.35, 1.3)
    segs = np.stack([J["xy"][:-1], J["xy"][1:]], axis=1)
    ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs, colors=DIVERGING(norm(np.clip(J["cp_s"], -1.6, 1))), linewidths=6, capstyle="butt", zorder=2))
    ax.plot(J["mid"][:, 0], J["mid"][:, 1], "o", ms=2.6, color=INK, zorder=3)
    plain = J["cp_s"].mean(); weighted = np.sum(J["w"] * J["cp_s"]) / J["w"].sum()
    ax.set_title(f"{title}: {len(J['w'])} cells")
    ax.text(0.0, -1.0, f"plain mean of $C_p$ over points: {plain:+.3f}", ha="center", fontsize=9.5, color=INK2)
    ax.text(0.0, -1.22, f"measure-weighted mean: {weighted:+.3f}", ha="center", fontsize=9.5, color=BLUE, fontweight="bold")
sm = plt.cm.ScalarMappable(norm=norm, cmap=DIVERGING); sm.set_array([])
cb = fig.colorbar(sm, ax=axes, fraction=0.025, pad=0.02); cb.set_label("surface pressure coefficient $C_p$ [–]", color=INK2)
plt.show()
```

In ISLA the measure enters every attention softmax over tokens as a
log-space bias, $\ell_i \equiv \log w_i$:

$$
\frac{\exp(\lambda_{is} + \ell_i)}{\sum_j \exp(\lambda_{js} + \ell_j)}
= \frac{w_i\, e^{\lambda_{is}}}{\sum_j w_j\, e^{\lambda_{js}}} .
$$

Here $\lambda_{is}$ is the learned score of token $i$ for slice $s$ (idea
3). The weight a slice gives a token is its area times a learned,
content-dependent factor, so every slice aggregate is a weighted quadrature
of the blue kind. When cells are drawn at random with unequal
probabilities, the data pipeline divides each area by its inclusion
probability (the Horvitz–Thompson weight, which a statistician would call
an importance weight), and the estimate stays unbiased. The measure is a
correctness requirement, not a knob: without it a slice averages over
whichever points the mesher placed, and a different mesher changes the
answer. @sec-principle states this as the acceptance criterion it is, and
@sec-sampling-laws draws the sampling laws the book uses.

## Idea 2: position without a frame {#sec-isla-frame}

**A model that is handed coordinates in some frame must learn that the
frame is arbitrary. ISLA is never handed coordinates.** It needs two things
in their place: a unit of length, and a way to say where a token is.

The unit of length is how far apart the boundary's points typically are.
Take every pair of points, weight the pair by the measure the two points
stand for, and average their squared separation; the square root is $L$.
With normalized weights $\tilde w_i \equiv w_i / \sum_j w_j$,

$$
L^2 \equiv \sum_{i,j} \tilde w_i \tilde w_j\, \lvert x_i - x_j\rvert^2
      = 2 \sum_i \tilde w_i\, \lvert x_i - \bar x\rvert^2 ,
\qquad r_i \equiv x_i / L ,
$$

where the second form, the variance identity, is what the code evaluates in
$O(N)$ (`rms_pairwise_distance` in `geometry.py`). $L$ is a property of the
boundary, not of the mesher, because the weights are areas. It needs no
center, because only differences of positions enter; the weighted mean
$\bar x$ appears inside this one scalar and nowhere else. It does not change
when every weight is multiplied by a constant. And it stays finite under
refinement of any boundary with a finite second moment, including a fractal
one whose total length diverges, which is why the unit is an RMS distance
and not, say, the square root of the total area. A uniform rescale of the
body is invisible to everything downstream of $r_i$.

Where a token is, ISLA states only *relative to other things*. The scaled
positions $r_i$ are used solely in differences $r_i - z_s$ against slice
anchors (idea 3), so a common shift of every point cancels exactly and
translation invariance needs no centering. The only data a token starts
with, its **seed**, is the orientation of its normal against each global
direction, together with the global scalars:

$$
s_i \equiv \big[\,\hat n_i\!\cdot\!\hat g_1,\ \dots,\ \hat n_i\!\cdot\!\hat g_K,\ \sigma\,\big],
\qquad h_i^{(0)} = \mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{embed}}(s_i) \in \mathbb{R}^{512} .
$$

On the airfoil the seed says "how much this cell faces the oncoming flow".
The embedding MLP lifts that to the token's 512-dimensional state $h_i$,
the vector the rest of the network refines. With $K = 0$ and $S = 0$ the
seed is a constant, and every distinction between tokens comes from their
relations to the anchors.

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-frame
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Why the frame must not be a point statistic. The two samplings of
#|   @fig-isla-quadrature overlaid. The plain mean of the sampled positions
#|   (open gray markers) moves toward the leading edge when the sampling is
#|   clustered there, so a model whose coordinates are centered on it would
#|   see the whole body displaced. The measure-weighted centroid (blue) and
#|   the length unit $L$ (printed) are integrals and agree between the
#|   samplings to quadrature error. How to read this: ISLA's slice layers use
#|   no center, only the length unit (ISLA-DTT's forest frame aside,
#|   @sec-arch-modes); the centroid is drawn to show that an
#|   integral is stable where a point statistic is not.
#| code-fold: true
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 3.6))
clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.4, 2.4); ax.set_ylim(-1.1, 1.2)
ax.plot(Ju["xy"][:, 0], Ju["xy"][:, 1], color=INK, lw=1.0)
cent = {}
for J, mk, lab in ((Ju, "o", "equal-arclength"), (Jm, "s", "clustered")):
    ax.plot(J["mid"][:, 0], J["mid"][:, 1], mk, ms=3.0, color=INK2 if mk == "o" else MUTED, alpha=0.8, label=f"{lab} sample points")
    cent[lab] = (J["mid"].mean(axis=0), (J["w"][:, None] * J["mid"]).sum(axis=0) / J["w"].sum())
    ax.plot(*cent[lab][0], mk, ms=11, mfc="white", mec=INK2, mew=2.0, zorder=5)
    ax.plot(*cent[lab][1], mk, ms=11, mfc=BLUE, mec=BLUE, mew=2.0, zorder=6)
ax.annotate("plain mean of the clustered sample:\npulled toward the leading edge", xy=cent["clustered"][0], xytext=(-1.6, -0.75),
            fontsize=8.5, color=INK2, ha="center", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=INK2, lw=0.8))
ax.annotate("measure-weighted centroids of both samplings\n(the equal-arclength plain mean coincides with them)", xy=cent["clustered"][1],
            xytext=(0.9, 0.75), fontsize=8.5, color=BLUE, ha="center", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=BLUE, lw=0.8))
def rms_pairwise(J):
    wt = J["w"] / J["w"].sum(); c = (wt[:, None] * J["mid"]).sum(axis=0)
    return np.sqrt(2.0 * np.sum(wt * np.sum((J["mid"] - c) ** 2, axis=1)))
ax.text(-2.3, -1.02, f"length unit $L$: {rms_pairwise(Ju):.3f} (equal-arclength), {rms_pairwise(Jm):.3f} (clustered)", fontsize=9, color=INK2)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8.5)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Optional: why the magnitude of a global vector is discarded"}
No fixed power of a far-field speed is a physical law of the output: a
pressure coefficient is homogeneous of degree zero in it, a dimensional
pressure of degree two, a skin-friction coefficient depends on it through
the Reynolds number. A model that read $g_k$ with its magnitude would have
to learn which power applies. ISLA reads the direction $\hat g_k$ and takes
any magnitude that matters as a global scalar, where the network learns its
role. In code: `gauge` is $L$, `r` is $r_i$, `n_hat` and `g_hat` are the
unit normal and directions, `log_w` is $\ell_i$, and `_seed_invariants` in
`model.py` builds the seed.
:::

## Idea 3: slices and their anchors {#sec-isla-slices}

**Slice attention routes every token softly into a few hundred slices, and
ISLA gives each slice a place: an anchor with a position and a facing
direction.** In each layer, a learned score $\lambda_{is}$ for every token
and slice and the measure bias of idea 1 give the routing weights, a
softmax over tokens:

$$
a_{is} = \frac{\exp(\lambda_{is} + \ell_i)}{\sum_j \exp(\lambda_{js} + \ell_j)},
\qquad \sum_i a_{is} = 1 .
$$

Each slice's weights sum to one over the tokens, so $\sum_i a_{is} f_i$ is a
quadrature average of $f$ over the slice's territory. In the language of
@sec-landscape, the $N \times M$ matrix $a$ is a learned *restriction* from
the fine level (tokens) to a coarse level of $M = 512$ slices. From the same
weights each slice forms two vectors,

$$
z_s \equiv \sum_i a_{is}\, r_i, \qquad
m_s \equiv \frac{\sum_i a_{is}\, \hat n_i}{\big\lvert \sum_i a_{is}\, \hat n_i \big\rvert},
$$

its mean position and its mean normal: the slice's **anchor**. Both are
weighted sums of vectors that rotate with the body, with weights that do
not, so the anchors rotate with the body. They give each layer 512
data-adaptive reference points with orientations. @fig-isla-slices draws
six of them on the airfoil.

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-slices
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Soft slices and their anchors, illustrated with six slices on the
#|   airfoil. Each cell is colored by the slice that gives it the most
#|   weight; the routing is a hand-made function of position along the
#|   surface, standing in for the learned scores. Stars are the anchors, the
#|   measure-weighted mean position of each slice, with the slice's mean
#|   normal as an arrow. How to read this: an anchor need not lie on the
#|   surface, and the assignment is soft (every cell has some weight in every
#|   slice); a layer of ISLA has 512 slices and learns its scores from the
#|   token states. The slice colors are labels only.
#| code-fold: true
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 3.8))
clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.5, 2.5); ax.set_ylim(-1.3, 1.4)
segs = np.stack([JJ["xy"][:-1], JJ["xy"][1:]], axis=1)
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs, colors=[SIX[k] for k in a6.argmax(axis=1)], linewidths=6, capstyle="butt", zorder=2))
for k in range(N_SL):
    ax.plot(*z6[k], marker="*", ms=16, color=SIX[k], mec=INK, mew=0.6, zorder=5)
    arrow(ax, z6[k], 0.45 * m6[k], SIX[k])
ax.text(0.0, -1.2, r"star: anchor position $z_s = \sum_i a_{is} r_i$;  arrow: anchor normal $m_s$", ha="center", fontsize=9.5, color=INK2)
plt.show()
```

### The routing score: a bounded cosine against sample-conditioned prototypes {#sec-isla-routing-forms}

**ISLA scores a token against a slice by a bounded cosine, so the routing
cannot sharpen without limit as its weights grow.** The score
reads the normalized token state $\tilde h_i \equiv \mathrm{LN}(h_i)$,
where LayerNorm (@sec-landscape) removes a vector's mean and scales it to
unit variance across its 512 components, and compares it with one
**prototype** $p_s$ per slice:

$$
\lambda_{is} = T\,\frac{\tilde h_i \cdot p_s}{\lVert \tilde h_i \rVert\,\lVert p_s \rVert},
\qquad T = 10 .
$$

Every content score lies in $[-10, 10]$, so the routing softmax can
sharpen only so far: within one slice, the weights of two tokens differ by
at most a factor $e^{20}$ beyond the ratio of their measures, however the
token states and prototypes grow. (The geometric refinement of idea 4 adds a
linear function of six geometric scalars on top; it sharpens the routing
only through its six learned weights.) An unbounded score, an affine map
$W\tilde h_i + b$, has no such ceiling. Under a step-size
schedule fit for a wide, deep network its weights grow, each slice's
softmax sharpens toward one token and each token's toward one slice, and a
sharper routing concentrates the slice states, which sharpens the next
layer's routing: a positive feedback loop whose gain rises with width and
depth. The bound cuts that loop.

The prototypes are not fixed rows of a weight matrix. Each is a learned
**seed** vector plus a summary of the sample in front of it: the seeds
attend over the token states with a measure-weighted softmax (a quadrature
again), the attended value is centered across the slices, and its size is
held smoothly below a learned fraction $g$ of the seeds' spread,

$$
p_s = \theta_s + \Delta^{c}_s\, \frac{b}{\mathrm{rms}(\Delta^{c}) + b},
\qquad b = g\, \mathrm{rms}(\theta), \qquad g = 0.1 \text{ at initialization},
$$

with $\theta_s$ the seeds and $\Delta^{c}$ the centered summary. So the
slices a layer offers adapt to the case, a car's slices to the car and a
bracket's to the bracket, while every score keeps its bound. Centering
removes the part of the summary common to every slice, which carries no
routing information under a cosine and, if it dominated, would pull every
prototype toward one direction.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Optional: why the routing softmax runs over tokens and the read-back over slices"}
Routing normalizes over tokens so that a slice is an *average*, with the
measure bias making it a quadrature average. Reading back (idea 5)
normalizes over slices, with no measure bias, because there a token is
choosing *where to read*, not how much it weighs. Adding a constant to
every $\ell_i$ cancels in the routing ratio and leaves $L$ unchanged, since
the weights are normalized before they enter it; so ISLA is invariant to a
rescale of the weights alone as well as to a joint geometric rescale.
:::

## Idea 4: relational invariants {#sec-isla-relational}

**Everything a token learns about its position, it learns from a handful of
scalars per anchor.** For each token–anchor pair, with
$\rho_{is} \equiv r_i - z_s$ the separation and $\hat\rho_{is}$ its
direction, the layer forms

$$
\xi_{is} \equiv \big[\,
\lvert\rho_{is}\rvert,\ \log\lvert\rho_{is}\rvert,\
\hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\!\hat g_1,\ \dots,\ \hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\!\hat g_K,\
\hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\!\hat n_i,\
\hat\rho_{is}\!\cdot\! m_s,\ \hat n_i\!\cdot\! m_s
\,\big],
$$

$5 + K$ numbers, six with one global direction. They say how far the anchor
is on two scales, whether it lies along or against the flow, whether it
lies in front of the token's face or behind it, whether the token lies in
front of the anchor's face, and whether the two faces agree. Each is a norm
or a dot product of vectors that rotate together, so each is unchanged by
any rotation, reflection or translation. @fig-isla-relational draws them for
one token and one anchor.

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-relational
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The relational invariants of one token against one anchor. The token
#|   (black dot) has normal $\hat n_i$; the anchor (star) has position $z_s$
#|   and normal $m_s$; the separation $\rho_{is}$ runs from anchor to token.
#|   The six scalars are the length of $\rho$, its logarithm, and four
#|   cosines, printed for this pair. How to read this: every one of these
#|   numbers is the same after any rotation or translation of the page; no
#|   coordinate axis appears in any of them.
#| code-fold: true
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 4.2))
clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.5, 2.5); ax.set_ylim(-1.5, 1.5)
airfoil(ax, JJ)
i, k = 22, 4
xi, ni = JJ["mid"][i], JJ["nrm"][i]; zs, ms = z6[k], m6[k]
rho = xi - zs; rho_hat = rho / np.linalg.norm(rho); g = JJ["g_hat"]
ax.plot(*xi, "o", ms=8, color=INK, zorder=6)
ax.plot(*zs, marker="*", ms=18, color=VIOLET, mec=INK, mew=0.6, zorder=6)
arrow(ax, zs, rho, INK2, 1.6); arrow(ax, xi, 0.5 * ni, INK); arrow(ax, zs, 0.5 * ms, VIOLET)
arrow(ax, np.array([-2.3, 1.05]), 0.6 * g, INK, 2.0)
ax.text(-2.3, 1.25, r"$\hat g_1$ (global direction)", fontsize=10, color=INK)
ax.text(*(xi + 0.62 * ni + [0.12, 0.0]), r"$\hat n_i$", fontsize=11, color=INK, ha="left", va="center", path_effects=halo())
ax.text(*(zs + 0.6 * ms + [0.0, -0.08]), r"$m_s$", fontsize=11, color=VIOLET, ha="center", va="top")
ax.text(*(zs + 0.5 * rho + [0.15, 0.0]), r"$\rho_{is} = r_i - z_s$", fontsize=11, color=INK2, ha="left", va="center", path_effects=halo())
ax.text(*(xi + [-0.12, 0.08]), "token $i$", fontsize=10, color=INK, ha="right", va="bottom", path_effects=halo())
ax.text(*(zs + [0.12, -0.08]), "anchor $s$", fontsize=10, color=VIOLET, ha="left", va="top", path_effects=halo())
vals = [(r"$|\rho_{is}|$", f"{np.linalg.norm(rho):.2f}"), (r"$\log|\rho_{is}|$", f"{np.log(np.linalg.norm(rho)):+.2f}"),
        (r"$\hat\rho_{is}\cdot\hat g_1$", f"{rho_hat @ g:+.2f}"), (r"$\hat\rho_{is}\cdot \hat n_i$", f"{rho_hat @ ni:+.2f}"),
        (r"$\hat\rho_{is}\cdot m_s$", f"{rho_hat @ ms:+.2f}"), (r"$\hat n_i\cdot m_s$", f"{ni @ ms:+.2f}")]
ax.text(1.35, 1.4, r"$\xi_{is}$, the six relational invariants", fontsize=9.5, color=INK, fontweight="bold")
for j, (lab, v) in enumerate(vals):
    ax.text(1.4, 1.15 - 0.27 * j, lab, fontsize=10, color=INK, va="center"); ax.text(2.45, 1.15 - 0.27 * j, v, fontsize=10, color=INK2, ha="right", va="center")
plt.show()
```

The invariants do two jobs in a layer. A learned linear map of $\xi_{is}$
to one scalar **refines the routing**,
$\lambda'_{is} = \lambda_{is} + w_g \cdot \xi_{is} + b_g$, so that a slice
can prefer tokens that are near its anchor, downstream of it, or facing it;
the routing weights $a'_{is}$ are recomputed with the refined scores. And
the invariants are **pooled back** to the token (idea 5), so it learns
where it sits relative to the slices it belongs to. Extra per-cell vector
inputs join the list the same way the normal does: a prescribed traction
$v_i$ contributes $v_i \cdot \hat\rho_{is}$, a prescribed stress $T_i$
contributes $\hat\rho_{is}^{\mathsf T} T_i \hat\rho_{is}$
(@sec-isla-inputs-rank).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Optional: what the first moments cannot see"}
The anchors are first moments of each slice's territory. Two non-congruent
arrangements of tokens with the same weighted means and mean normals in
every slice are indistinguishable to a layer. Twelve layers with different
routings make such a collision unlikely on real geometry, and no measured
deficit in this book has been traced to one, but the representation is not
complete in the sense of an invariant theory; it is a practical, cheap set
of invariants.
:::

## Idea 5: the slice layer, assembled {#sec-isla-layer}

**A slice layer sends information up from tokens to slices, transforms it
there, and sends it back down together with the geometry.** With the
refined routing weights, the slice state is the quadrature mean of the
normalized token states, passed through a per-slice MLP (the slices'
private computation):

$$
Z_s = \sum_i a'_{is}\, \tilde h_i, \qquad Z_s \leftarrow Z_s + \mathrm{MLP}_{\mathrm{slice}}(\mathrm{LN}(Z_s)).
$$

Reading back, the *prolongation* of @sec-landscape, uses a softmax over
slices for each token, with no measure bias, and pools both the slice
states and the relational invariants:

$$
\pi_{is} = \frac{\exp(\lambda'_{is})}{\sum_t \exp(\lambda'_{it})}, \qquad
b_i = \sum_s \pi_{is}\, Z_s, \qquad
\gamma_i = W_f \Big(\sum_s \pi_{is}\, \xi_{is}\Big) + b_f .
$$

The token's state is then updated twice, each time by adding to it:

$$
h_i \leftarrow h_i + W_b\,[\,\tilde h_i;\ b_i;\ \gamma_i\,], \qquad
h_i \leftarrow h_i + \mathrm{MLP}(\mathrm{LN}(h_i)) .
$$

The token ends the layer knowing which slices it belongs to, what those
slices contain, and where it sits relative to their anchors. Twelve such
layers make the encoder. @fig-isla-layer-flow draws one layer as a flow.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-isla-layer-flow
%%| fig-cap: >
%%|   One slice layer as a flow. Gray boxes are data, blue boxes learned maps,
%%|   dashed boxes fixed geometric maps. The raw state $h$ enters only the two
%%|   residual additions and the token MLP's LayerNorm; every read of the slice
%%|   sublayer is of the normalized state $\tilde h$. How to read this: arrows
%%|   carry tensors of shape (tokens, width) or (slices, width), not
%%|   coordinates; the exact shapes and code are in @sec-arch-layer.
flowchart TD
  h["token state h"]:::data --> ln["LayerNorm: LN(h)"]:::learned
  ln --> score["scores λ: cosine vs prototypes"]:::learned
  ln -. "LN(h)" .-> pool
  ln -. "LN(h)" .-> add1
  score --> route["routing a: softmax over tokens, + log w"]:::fixed
  route --> anchors["anchors z, m"]:::fixed
  anchors --> inv["invariants ξ"]:::fixed
  inv --> refine["refined routing a′, read-back π"]:::learned
  refine --> pool["slice states Z = Σ a′ LN(h), then the slice MLP"]:::learned
  pool --> back["read back b = Σ π Z, γ = W Σ π ξ"]:::learned
  back --> add1(("h + W [LN(h); b; γ]")):::data
  h -. residual .-> add1
  add1 --> mlp["h + MLP(LN(h))"]:::learned
  classDef data fill:#f4f3ee,stroke:#898781;
  classDef learned fill:#e6f0fb,stroke:#2a78d6;
  classDef fixed fill:#ffffff,stroke:#2a78d6,stroke-dasharray:4 3;
```

The projection $W_f$ of the pooled invariants is applied *after* pooling,
which is exact because the projection is affine and $\pi_{is}$ sums to one
over slices; it saves storing a (tokens × slices × width) tensor, the
largest object the layer would otherwise hold (@sec-arch-layer).

### Why the slice sublayer reads the normalized state {#sec-isla-normalized-reads}

**Every read of the slice sublayer is of $\tilde h_i$, never of $h_i$
itself, so each layer adds a bounded update to the token state instead of
multiplying it.** This is the one place where the architecture is shaped by
how it trains, and the reason is worth a careful look, because it is
dynamics an optimization theorist will recognize.

The token state $h_i$ is a *residual stream*: each layer adds its update
to it, $h^{(k+1)} = h^{(k)} + F_k(h^{(k)})$, so the network is a
composition of near-identity maps and its end-to-end Jacobian is the
product $\prod_k (I + \partial F_k / \partial h)$. Whether that product
stays tame depends on how the update depends on the stream's size. Suppose
the broadcast read the raw state, $F_k(h) = W_b\,[\,h;\ b;\ \gamma\,]$.
Then the update contains the term $W_h h$, linear in $h$, and the layer map
is $h \mapsto (I + W_h)\,h + \dots$: the stream is multiplied by $I + W_h$
at every layer. Twelve layers with a gain of 1.5 each amplify the stream
130-fold per forward pass. Training makes it worse, because nothing pulls
$\lVert I + W_h \rVert$ back toward one. ISLA trains its matrices with
Muon, which is steepest descent in the spectral norm: every step moves each
weight matrix by a fixed spectral-norm step, the orthogonalized direction
of the momentum, regardless of the gradient's magnitude (@sec-using-lr).
Steps that keep a fixed size let the layer gains drift upward over tens of
thousands of steps, and the stream's norm grows geometrically in the
product of those gains.

A geometrically growing stream does damage a long way before it overflows.
The network trains in bfloat16, a 16-bit format with an 8-bit mantissa: an
update smaller than about $2^{-8}$ of the number it is added to is rounded
away. When the stream has grown by orders of magnitude, the deep layers'
updates fall below that threshold and those layers stop contributing,
silently. With the normalized read, $F_k$ depends on $h$ only through
$\tilde h = \mathrm{LN}(h)$, which has unit RMS whatever $\lVert h \rVert$
is, so $\lVert F_k(h) \rVert$ is bounded independently of the stream's size
and the stream grows at most additively, by a bounded amount per layer.
@fig-isla-stream-toy shows both behaviors on a toy stack with random
weights.

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-stream-toy
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Why a raw read compounds and a normalized read does not. Top: a
#|   12-layer stack whose every layer amplifies a unit-size stream by a factor
#|   $g$. If the update reads the raw state, each layer multiplies the stream
#|   by $g$ whatever its size, and 12 layers give $g^{12}$ (gray, dashed). If
#|   it reads the normalized state, the update has the same size as at unit
#|   state, $g - 1$, however large the stream already is, and 12 layers add at
#|   most $12(g - 1)$ (blue, solid). Bottom: what bfloat16 arithmetic does to an update $\delta$ of
#|   relative size $\lVert\delta\rVert/\lVert h\rVert$ added to a random
#|   state $h$: the fraction of the update's components that change the sum.
#|   How to read this: the top panel is arithmetic and the bottom one is
#|   computed here from random numbers; neither is a measurement of ISLA. The
#|   measurements on trained models are in @tbl-aerozoo-training and
#|   @sec-surface-deepjeb.
#| fig-height: 6.2
#| code-fold: true
import torch
from matplotlib.ticker import FuncFormatter
depth = 12
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 6.0), gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.45))
ax = axes[0]
g = np.linspace(1.0, 1.6, 121)
ax.plot(g, g ** depth, ls="--", color=MUTED, lw=2.0)
ax.plot(g, 1 + depth * (g - 1), ls="-", color=BLUE, lw=2.2)
ax.text(1.42, 1.42 ** depth * 1.6, r"raw read: $\|h^{(12)}\| = g^{12}$", color=INK2, fontsize=9.5, ha="right", path_effects=halo())
ax.text(1.45, 2.4, r"normalized read: at most $1 + 12\,(g - 1)$", color=BLUE, fontsize=9.5, ha="center", path_effects=halo())
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_xlim(1.0, 1.6)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:g}")); ax.yaxis.set_minor_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: ""))
ax.set_xlabel("per-layer amplification of a unit stream, $g$ [–]"); ax.set_ylabel("stream size after\n12 layers [–]")
ax = axes[1]
rel = np.logspace(-4.5, -0.5, 60)
hb = torch.randn(200_000, dtype=torch.float32)
surv = []
for r in rel:
    d = torch.randn_like(hb) * float(r)
    kept = ((hb.bfloat16() + d.bfloat16()).float() - hb.bfloat16().float()) != 0
    surv.append(kept.float().mean().item())
ax.semilogx(rel, surv, color=INK, lw=2.0)
ax.axvline(2.0 ** -8, color=BASELINE, ls="--", lw=1.2)
ax.text(2.0 ** -8 * 1.15, 0.12, "$2^{-8}$, the unit roundoff of bfloat16", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2)
ax.set_xlabel(r"relative update size $\|\delta\| / \|h\|$ [–]"); ax.set_ylabel("share of the update's\ncomponents kept [–]")
ax.set_ylim(-0.02, 1.02)
plt.show()
```

The normalized read is the full meaning of "pre-LN" for a sublayer whose
inputs are read in several places: routing, pooling and broadcast all read
$\tilde h$, and the raw $h$ enters the layer only through the residual
identity and the token MLP's own LayerNorm. On ISLA trained at its single
learning rate, the effect is measured directly (@fig-isla-stream).

### What the trained routing looks like {#sec-arch-routing-trained}

**On a trained model a slice is a soft region of the body: the first
layer barely routes, a few middle layers cut the surface into patches such
as the wheels, and the last layers spread the mass over most of the slices
again, with every token's weight shared among many of them.** Every routing picture so far drew
hand-made weights. This section reads the real ones out of trained
checkpoints. The instrument records the refined routing scores of every
layer on one validation case. From them, each token's **soft assignment**
is its read-back weight vector $\pi_{is}$; its **dominant slice** is
$\arg\max_s \pi_{is}$; a slice's **mass** is
$q_s \equiv \frac{1}{N}\sum_i \pi_{is}$; and the **effective number of
slices** is $M_{\mathrm{eff}} \equiv \exp(-\sum_s q_s \log q_s)$, which
equals the slice count when every slice carries the same mass and 1 when
one slice carries all of it.

```{python}
#| label: setup-routing-trained
#| include: false
import json
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
SL = RES / "renderings_2026-10-18" / "routing"
PF = RES / "problem_figures_2026-09-22"
M_SL = 512

def load_slices(run, n_draw=60000):
    """One routing probe; the per-token arrays are thinned to a fixed subset of n_draw tokens for drawing."""
    z = np.load(SL / f"{run}.npz"); meta = json.load(open(SL / f"{run}.json"))
    d = {k: z[k] for k in z.files}
    if len(d["keep"]) > n_draw:
        sub = np.sort(np.random.default_rng(0).choice(len(d["keep"]), n_draw, replace=False))
        d["keep"] = d["keep"][sub]
        for k in ("dominant", "pi_max"):
            d[k] = d[k][:, sub]
        for k in ("top_pi", "top_a_density"):
            d[k] = d[k][:, sub]
    return d, meta

def n_eff(q):
    return float(np.exp(-(q * np.log(q + 1e-30)).sum()))

SLICE_COLS = slice_colors(M_SL)

def partition_colors(dom, conf, floor=0.25):
    """Dominant-slice color, faded toward paper where the token is undecided (its largest pi_is is small)."""
    c = SLICE_COLS[dom].copy(); a = np.clip(conf / max(np.quantile(conf, 0.95), 1e-6), floor, 1.0)
    paper = np.array([0.96, 0.96, 0.95, 1.0])
    return a[:, None] * c + (1 - a[:, None]) * paper

def draw_anchors(ax, d, li, scale=1.0, dims=(0, 1), s=50):
    q = d["q"][li]; active = np.flatnonzero(q > 1.0 / M_SL); A = d["anchors"][li][active] * scale
    ax.scatter(A[:, dims[0]], A[:, dims[1]], marker="*", s=s, c=SLICE_COLS[active], edgecolors=INK, linewidths=0.45, zorder=5)
    return len(active)

DR, DRm = load_slices("a2r_dr_isla_seed42_s00079")
AF, AFm = load_slices("afu_a2s_isla_seed42_s00215")
LG, LGm = load_slices("a2r_lug_isla_seed42_s00633")
L_REF_DR = json.load(open(PF / "drivaer.json"))["L_ref"]        # the recipe divides DrivAerML positions by L_ref = 5 m
NE_DR = [n_eff(DR["q"][li]) for li in range(12)]
L_PEAK = int(np.argmin(NE_DR))       # the layer whose routing is most concentrated
```

## Idea 6: fields of any rank from an equivariant basis {#sec-isla-heads}

**The network's state is made of invariants, so an output of tensor rank
$r$ is assembled from tensor products of $r$ vectors that rotate with the
body, with invariant coefficients.** One linear head on the normalized
final state produces every output's coefficients, and an output of rank $r$
is their contraction with products of $r$ vectors from the token's
**basis**:

$$
c_i = W_o\, \mathrm{LN}(h_i), \qquad
T_i = \sum_{j_1 \dots j_r} c_{i\,j_1 \dots j_r}\,
t_{i j_1} \otimes \dots \otimes t_{i j_r} \;+\; \text{isotropic terms},
$$

$$
\{t_{ij}\} = \big\{\hat g_1, \dots, \hat g_K,\ \hat n_i,\ \hat u_i,\
e_\theta(\hat u_i, \hat n_i),\ e_\theta(\hat u_i, \hat g_1), \dots, e_\theta(\hat u_i, \hat g_K)\big\} .
$$

Rank 0 is the coefficient itself (pressure). Rank 1 is a combination of the
$m = 2K + 3$ basis vectors: five coefficients for wall shear stress with one
global direction. A symmetric rank 2 output is a combination of the
$m(m+1)/2$ symmetrized outer products plus the identity: sixteen
coefficients for a stress tensor with one global direction. Three of the
basis vectors are directions the token already has: the global directions,
its normal, and $\hat u_i$, the **radial** direction from the token's own
soft anchor (a separate routing assigns the token to slices, and
$u_i = r_i - \sum_s \beta_{is} z_s$ is a difference of positions, so no
center appears). The complements $e_\theta(\hat u, \hat a)$, the part of
$-\hat a$ orthogonal to $\hat u$, keep the expansion well conditioned where
the three primary directions are nearly coplanar; they are left
unnormalized, so they vanish smoothly where $\hat u \parallel \hat a$, and
no direction field on a sphere ever has to be combed. Every basis vector is
a true vector, so every product is a true tensor and the output transforms
as $R^{\otimes r}$ under rotations *and* reflections. @fig-isla-basis
draws the basis at one token.

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-basis
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The vector head's basis at one token, in the plane of the airfoil. A
#|   predicted vector, such as the wall shear stress, is a combination with
#|   learned invariant coefficients of directions the token owns: the global
#|   direction $\hat g_1$, its normal $\hat n_i$, the radial direction
#|   $\hat u_i$ from its soft anchor (star), and the complement $e_\theta$.
#|   How to read this: rotate the page and every basis vector rotates with
#|   it while the coefficients, being invariants, do not; that is the whole
#|   of the covariance proof. It does not show a trained head.
#| code-fold: true
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.0, 3.8))
clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.5, 2.5); ax.set_ylim(-1.3, 1.5)
airfoil(ax, JJ)
i = 18; xi, ni = JJ["mid"][i], JJ["nrm"][i]; g = JJ["g_hat"]
beta = np.exp(-((s_mid[i] - centers) / (0.35 * total)) ** 2); beta /= beta.sum()
anchor = (beta[:, None] * z6).sum(axis=0); u = xi - anchor; u_hat = u / np.linalg.norm(u)
e_th = -(ni - (ni @ u_hat) * u_hat); e_th_hat = e_th / np.linalg.norm(e_th)
ax.plot(*anchor, marker="*", ms=16, color=VIOLET, mec=INK, mew=0.6, zorder=6)
ax.plot(*xi, "o", ms=8, color=INK, zorder=6)
arrow(ax, anchor, u, INK2, 1.2)
for v, c, lab in ((g, INK, r"$\hat g_1$"), (ni, BLUE, r"$\hat n_i$"), (u_hat, VIOLET, r"$\hat u_i$"), (e_th_hat, AQUA, r"$e_\theta(\hat u_i,\hat n_i)$")):
    arrow(ax, xi, 0.6 * v, c, 2.0); ax.text(*(xi + 0.75 * v), lab, fontsize=11, color=c, ha="center", va="center", path_effects=halo())
ax.annotate("token's soft anchor", xy=anchor, xytext=(anchor[0] - 0.9, -0.75), fontsize=9, color=VIOLET, ha="center",
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=VIOLET, lw=0.7), path_effects=halo())
ax.annotate(r"$u_i = r_i - \sum_s \beta_{is} z_s$", xy=anchor + 0.5 * u, xytext=(anchor[0] + 1.3, -0.75), fontsize=9.5, color=INK2,
            ha="center", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=INK2, lw=0.7), path_effects=halo())
ax.text(0.2, -1.15, r"$v_i = \sum_j c_{ij}\, t_{ij}$: invariant coefficients $c_{ij}$ times body-fixed directions $t_{ij}$", ha="center", fontsize=9.5, color=INK2)
plt.show()
```

**A tensor component is only ever a view of a tensor.** A scalar head can
represent only invariants of the input vector set, and a stress component
$\sigma_{xy} = e_x^{\mathsf T} \sigma\, e_y$ is not an invariant of that set:
it needs the laboratory axes $e_x, e_y$. ISLA therefore predicts the tensor
itself, declared with its rank (`stress: {rank: 2, symmetric: true}`), and
the components are read off it afterwards. No laboratory frame enters
anywhere. Passing the dataset's axes as extra global directions would also
keep the algebra covariant if the axes rotated with every case; held fixed,
as a dataset stores them, they are not a datum of the PDE but the pose of
the training set, and a model that needs them has been told it
(@sec-pose-inputs).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Optional: reflections and pseudotensors"}
Every invariant in the network is a norm or a dot product of true vectors,
so every scalar output is unchanged by a mirror as well as a rotation, and
every even-parity output is a true tensor. A quantity that flips sign under
a mirror (a vorticity, a torque) is a pseudotensor and is declared with
`parity: odd`. Its basis is the set of products with exactly one
*pseudovector* factor: in three dimensions the cross products of the primary
directions $\hat g_k, \hat n_i, \hat u_i$, $\binom{K+2}{2}$ of them (three
with one global direction); in two dimensions their perpendiculars. Such an
output transforms as $\det(R)\, R^{\otimes r}$, the pseudotensor law. The
parity is a declaration, so a true vector never pays for a pseudovector's
basis. The library's tests hold the covariance to $10^{-12}$ in float64 for
random rotations and mirrors at every rank and parity the class admits.
:::

### Inputs of any rank enter through invariants {#sec-isla-inputs-rank}

**The same rule runs backwards at the input: a boundary field of rank 1 or
2 reaches the network only through its invariants against directions the
token already has.** A per-cell vector $v_i$ (a prescribed traction)
contributes to the seed its cosines with the token's frame,
$v_i \cdot \hat n_i$ and $v_i \cdot \hat g_k$, its norm, and its dot products
with the token's other vector inputs; inside every layer it contributes
$v_i \cdot \hat\rho_{is}$ beside $\hat n_i \cdot \hat\rho_{is}$. A per-cell
rank-2 field $T_i$ (a prescribed stress) contributes the bilinear forms
$a^{\mathsf T} T_i b$ over $a, b \in \{\hat n_i, \hat g_k\}$, its trace and
its Frobenius norm to the seed, and $\hat\rho^{\mathsf T} T_i \hat\rho$,
$\hat\rho \cdot T_i \hat n_i$, $\hat\rho \cdot T_i \hat g_k$ inside every
layer. Only true vectors appear on the input side, so every input invariant
is unchanged by a mirror, and pseudotensor inputs are refused. A dataset
that stores a vector component by component stacks the components into one
rank-1 field before ISLA sees it; feeding laboratory components as scalars
would leak the frame.

## Idea 7: predicting inside the domain {#sec-isla-interior}

**On an interior task the prediction points join the boundary cells as
tokens, and each one is told only how far it is from the wall and in which
direction.** A surface task predicts at the cells it was given. An interior
task (a velocity field around a car, a stress field in a bracket) predicts
at points $x_q$ off the boundary, and a point has no normal and no area. ISLA
gives each prediction point the two geometric facts a PDE solver would use
there, computed inside the model from the boundary tokens: the **signed
distance** to the wall and the **direction** to it. For each $x_q$, an
exact search finds the nearest boundary token $y_{i^*}$, and

$$
d_q = \pm\, \lvert x_q - y_{i^*} \rvert, \qquad \hat\nu_q = \frac{x_q - y_{i^*}}{\lvert x_q - y_{i^*} \rvert},
$$

signed by that token's normal. The direction $\hat\nu_q$ plays the role of
the normal in every invariant (the seed's $\hat\nu_q \cdot \hat g_k$, the
layers' $\hat\rho_{qs} \cdot \hat\nu_q$), and the distance enters the
point's embedding as $d_q/L$ and its signed logarithm, so that the boundary
layer, where $d_q/L$ is tiny, is resolved on a log scale.
@fig-isla-interior draws both on the airfoil.

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-interior
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The geometry a prediction point receives, on the running airfoil with
#|   40 boundary cells. Top: points of a grid around the airfoil, colored by
#|   their distance to the nearest boundary token in units of the length
#|   unit $L$ (positive outside the body, where every point here lies); thin
#|   aqua lines join a few points to that token. Bottom: the error of that
#|   distance against the exact distance to the curve, near the leading
#|   edge, in the same units. How to read this: far from the wall the
#|   nearest-token distance is the exact one; within about one cell length
#|   of the wall it overestimates by up to half a cell, in a sawtooth that
#|   follows the sample. A finer or different boundary sample changes that
#|   error, which is why this is the one input of ISLA that depends on the
#|   discretization. It does not show a trained model.
#| fig-height: 6.8
#| code-fold: true
from matplotlib.path import Path as MPath
J = joukowski(n_cells=40); L_ = rms_pairwise(J)
Jf = joukowski(n_cells=8000)                                   # the curve, finely, for the exact distance
body = MPath(J["xy"])
gx, gy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-2.6, 2.7, 140), np.linspace(-1.3, 1.3, 70))
Xq = np.stack([gx.ravel(), gy.ravel()], 1)
Xq = Xq[~MPath(Jf["xy"]).contains_points(Xq)]
def nearest(X, P):
    d2 = ((X[:, None, :] - P[None]) ** 2).sum(-1); k = d2.argmin(1)
    return np.sqrt(d2[np.arange(len(X)), k]), k
d_tok, k_tok = nearest(Xq, J["mid"]); d_ex, _ = nearest(Xq, Jf["mid"])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 7.4), gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.25, height_ratios=[1.0, 1.25]))
ax = axes[0]; clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.6, 2.75); ax.set_ylim(-1.3, 1.3)
sc = ax.scatter(Xq[:, 0], Xq[:, 1], c=d_tok / L_, s=4, cmap=SEQUENTIAL, norm=mpl.colors.LogNorm(vmin=0.01, vmax=1.0), zorder=2, rasterized=True)
for q in np.random.default_rng(3).choice(len(Xq), 14, replace=False):
    ax.plot([Xq[q, 0], J["mid"][k_tok[q], 0]], [Xq[q, 1], J["mid"][k_tok[q], 1]], color=AQUA, lw=1.0, zorder=3)
    ax.plot(*Xq[q], "o", ms=3.5, color=AQUA, zorder=4)
airfoil(ax, J, color=INK, lw=1.2); ax.plot(J["mid"][:, 0], J["mid"][:, 1], "o", ms=2.5, color=INK, zorder=4)
cb = fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, fraction=0.03, pad=0.01); cb.outline.set_visible(False); cb.set_label("$d_q / L$ [–]")
ax.set_title("distance to the nearest boundary token", fontsize=9.5)
ax = axes[1]; clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.25, -0.85); ax.set_ylim(-0.32, 0.42)
gx2, gy2 = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-2.25, -0.85, 300), np.linspace(-0.32, 0.42, 170))
X2 = np.stack([gx2.ravel(), gy2.ravel()], 1); X2 = X2[~MPath(Jf["xy"]).contains_points(X2)]
e = (nearest(X2, J["mid"])[0] - nearest(X2, Jf["mid"])[0]) / L_
sc2 = ax.scatter(X2[:, 0], X2[:, 1], c=e, s=3, cmap=SEQUENTIAL, vmin=0, vmax=np.quantile(e, 0.995), zorder=2, rasterized=True)
airfoil(ax, J, color=INK, lw=1.2); ax.plot(J["mid"][:, 0], J["mid"][:, 1], "o", ms=4, color=INK, zorder=4)
cb = fig.colorbar(sc2, ax=ax, fraction=0.03, pad=0.01); cb.outline.set_visible(False); cb.set_label("overestimate / $L$ [–]")
ax.set_title("its error against the exact distance, near the leading edge", fontsize=9.5)
plt.show()
```

The nearest-token geometry is exact in the sense of the code (a brute-force
search, no approximation), but it is a function of the boundary *sample*:
near the wall it overestimates the true distance by up to about half a
sample spacing, and a different draw of boundary cells moves it. It is the one
input of ISLA that depends on the discretization; @sec-invariances measures
what that costs, and @sec-open-questions states what would replace it.

**Prediction points come in two kinds.** In ISLA's default interior form
the prediction points are **interacting** tokens: they carry routing mass,
a learned fraction of the total boundary measure split equally among them,
so they help form the slices and their anchors, and the prediction at one
point depends on which other points are in the request. That dependence is
the price of letting the interior shape the latent partition. ISLA-DTT
(`query_independent=True`) makes the points **read-only**: they carry no
routing mass, so at every layer they read the slices the boundary formed
and never write into them, and after every layer each point also reads
every boundary cell directly, through a learned kernel of the pair's
relative geometry and an attention over the cells' states, weighted by each
cell's share of the boundary measure. A Barnes–Hut tree makes that read
affordable: nearby cells are read one by one and a distant cluster of
cells as one virtual cell (its measure-weighted mean position, normal,
key and value), exactly as an N-body code treats a far cluster by its
monopole. The prediction at a point is then a function of that point and
the boundary alone: any request can be split into pieces with the same
answer. @fig-isla-dtt shows one point's read on the airfoil.

```{python}
#| label: fig-isla-dtt
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Two kinds of prediction point, on the airfoil. Left: an interacting
#|   point (ISLA's default, aqua) adds its weight to the slices (solid
#|   arrows into the anchors) and reads them back (dashed arrows), so the
#|   interior helps shape the partition. Right: a read-only point of ISLA-DTT
#|   reads the boundary through a tree over 160 cells: the cells near it one
#|   by one (black segments) and each distant cluster as one virtual cell
#|   (violet diamonds at the cluster's measure-weighted centroid, area
#|   proportional to the cluster's measure), a cluster being admitted when
#|   its size is below $\theta = 1$ times its distance to the point. How to
#|   read this: a schematic of the access pattern with a simple bisection
#|   tree; the model's forest also separates cells whose normals point in
#|   different octants, which this picture omits.
#| code-fold: true
J = joukowski(n_cells=160)
P_ = J["mid"]; Wc = J["w"]
def build(idx):
    node = dict(idx=idx, c=(Wc[idx, None] * P_[idx]).sum(0) / Wc[idx].sum())
    lo, hi = P_[idx].min(0), P_[idx].max(0); node["diag"] = float(np.linalg.norm(hi - lo))
    if len(idx) > 4:
        ax_ = int(np.argmax(hi - lo)); o = idx[np.argsort(P_[idx, ax_])]; h_ = len(o) // 2
        node["kids"] = [build(o[:h_]), build(o[h_:])]
    return node
root = build(np.arange(len(P_)))
k0 = 118; xq = P_[k0] + 0.06 * J["nrm"][k0]
near, far = [], []
def walk(nd):
    if nd["diag"] < 1.0 * np.linalg.norm(xq - nd["c"]):
        far.append(nd); return
    if "kids" in nd:
        for k_ in nd["kids"]: walk(k_)
    else:
        near.extend(nd["idx"].tolist())
walk(root)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.4, 3.6), gridspec_kw=dict(wspace=0.04))
ax = axes[0]; clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.4, 2.4); ax.set_ylim(-1.3, 1.3)
airfoil(ax, J, color=INK2)
for k in range(N_SL):
    ax.plot(*z6[k], marker="*", ms=12, color=VIOLET, mec=INK, mew=0.5, zorder=5)
q = np.array([0.9, 0.85]); ax.plot(*q, "o", ms=8, color=AQUA, zorder=6)
for k in (1, 3, 5):
    d_ = z6[k] - q; nrm_ = np.array([-d_[1], d_[0]]) / np.linalg.norm(d_) * 0.05
    ax.annotate("", xy=z6[k] + nrm_, xytext=q + nrm_, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=AQUA, lw=1.3), zorder=4)
    ax.annotate("", xy=q - nrm_, xytext=z6[k] - nrm_, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=AQUA, lw=1.0, ls="--"), zorder=4)
ax.text(0.95, 1.0, "writes and reads", fontsize=9, color=AQUA, path_effects=halo())
ax.set_title("interacting point: writes into the slices", fontsize=9.5)
ax = axes[1]; clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.4, 2.4); ax.set_ylim(-1.0, 1.0)
segs = np.stack([J["xy"][:-1], J["xy"][1:]], axis=1)
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs, colors=["#d9d4f2"], linewidths=3, zorder=1))
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs[near], colors=[INK], linewidths=3.5, zorder=2))
for nd in far:
    ax.plot([xq[0], nd["c"][0]], [xq[1], nd["c"][1]], color=VIOLET, lw=0.6, alpha=0.5, zorder=2)
    ax.plot(*nd["c"], "D", ms=3 + 12 * np.sqrt(Wc[nd["idx"]].sum() / Wc.sum()), color=VIOLET, mec=WHITE, mew=0.6, zorder=4)
ax.plot(*xq, "o", ms=8, color=AQUA, zorder=6)
ax.text(0.0, -0.92, f"{len(near)} cells read one by one, {len(far)} clusters as one virtual cell each, of {len(P_)}",
        ha="center", fontsize=8.8, color=INK2)
ax.set_title("read-only point: near cells exactly, far clusters by monopole", fontsize=9.5)
plt.show()
```

Which interior form a task should use is one of the questions the
AeroZoo benchmark decides (@sec-open-questions). On the datasets of this
book, the interior standings are ISLA's interacting form, and ISLA-DTT
appears where its own measurement exists.

## Why ISLA has no center {#sec-isla-variants}

**ISLA states position only relative to its own anchors because a PDE does
not know what "the body" is.** The area-weighted centroid of a surface is
not a point the physics distinguishes. For an open or truncated boundary, a
multi-body scene, or a boundary with structure at every scale, the centroid
is an artifact of where the domain was cut, and a frame built on it would
carry that artifact into every invariant. A center taken from a sample
statistic is worse still, since it moves with the mesher
(@fig-isla-frame). The relative construction presumes none of this:
positions enter only as differences against anchors that are themselves
quadrature means, and the one mean position in the model sits inside the
scalar $L$. One component is the exception, and it is an implementation
device rather than an input: ISLA-DTT builds its Barnes–Hut forest in a
frame the boundary carries (its measure-weighted centroid and principal
axes, signed by the third moments), so that every pose of a case gets the
same clusters; where that frame ties, on a body with equal principal
variances or a symmetric axis, the far-field approximation can differ
between poses (@sec-arch-modes). The two properties the relative
construction buys, pose and discretization, are the subject of
@sec-invariances.

## The forward pass on one page {#sec-isla-forward}

**Every symbol of the seven ideas has one identifier in the code, and
@sec-architecture is the dictionary.** @tbl-isla-ideas maps the ideas onto
the stages of that chapter.

| idea | what it is | stage of @sec-architecture | code |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 quadrature | the measure as a log-bias in every softmax over tokens | 3, 4 | `log_w` |
| 2 position without a frame | the length unit $L$; the seed | 1, 2 | `rms_pairwise_distance`, `_seed_invariants` |
| 3 slices and anchors | bounded cosine routing against prototypes; $z_s$, $m_s$ | 3 | `_RoutingLogits`, `_SliceBlock` |
| 4 relational invariants | $\xi_{is}$; the routing refinement | 3 | `_relational_invariants`, `geo_kernel.py` |
| 5 the slice layer | pooling, slice MLP, read-back, normalized reads | 3 | `_SliceBlock.forward` |
| 6 the equivariant basis | coefficients times body-fixed directions | 4, 5 | `heads.py`, `frame_assign` |
| 7 the interior | nearest-token geometry; interacting or read-only points | 1, 3 | `nearest_boundary_geometry`, `_QueryTokens`, `tree_read.py` |

: The seven ideas of this chapter, the stage of the forward pass that holds
each, and the code that implements it. How to read this: the stage numbers
refer to @fig-isla-pass; the code identifiers are in
`physicsnemo/experimental/models/isla/`. {#tbl-isla-ideas}
